paras: The attempted lynching of dining-car porters at Raton was an attack by a mob of nearly two hundred men on the Colfax County jail at Raton, New Mexico Territory, on the night of June 11, 1903, aimed at five Black porters held for the fatal shooting of Night Marshal John Jones. The sheriff had already removed the prisoners, who reached the Las Vegas jail unharmed, and New Mexico editors cited the case, and the jailing of two mob leaders, as proof of fitness for statehood.

Floods held several trains at Raton in early June, and porters from them went into town. Trainmen quoted by the Las Vegas Daily Optic said five porters who had been drinking were refused craps because "the rules of the saloon forbid colored men from gambling," and that Marshal Jones knocked two of them down before one fired at him. A wire dispatch said instead that three Black men "persisted in insulting Jones" and that one shot him from behind a saloon screen when he tried to arrest them.

Jones was shot about 11:30 on the night of June 10 and, by the Optic's account, died at 3 a.m.; the porter accused of firing was named as W. M. Mimms. The next day a "posse of 200 armed citizens" hunted the fugitive, who the Santa Fe New Mexican said "will be lynched if caught," and by afternoon officers had five men in jail amid open talk of lynching.

Warned that a mob was forming, with men from Trinidad, Colorado, to join it, Sheriff Marion Littrell took the prisoners out a back door at about 8:30 p.m.; with Deputy Nail he brought them to Las Vegas by train the next morning. At about ten o'clock "a mob of nearly two hundred men attacked the jail," forced a door and found the prisoners gone; one report named A. C. Webber as the man who broke the door with a sledge hammer. Some sixty Colorado men arrived near 2 a.m., too late, and Littrell told the Optic that the prisoners "all would have been lynched" had the mob secured them.

The day after the killing, white workers at the Santa Fe Railway round house at Raton drove the Black workmen away "with picks, shovels, and similar weapons." By June 18 Webber and W. L. Johnson, a boiler maker said to have urged the crowd to "come on," were jailed to await the grand jury, and a third leader had left town. At the fall term at Raton, William Minns, the porter accused of the shooting, received ninety-nine years for murder, and Webber and William M. Johnson one year each for burglary of the jail.
Distant papers ran a short Raton wire calling the shooting "most cold-blooded" under headlines such as "Mob After a Negro," "Mob Chasing Negro" and "Three Negroes in Danger."

Closer to home, the Santa Fe New Mexican's first headline predicted "A Lynching Bee Will Probably Be the Outcome," while the Optic called the accused "the colored boy who murdered Night Marshal Jones" but treated a lynching as a "disgrace" and printed the trainmen's account of the saloon's color rule, which the wire omitted.

Territorial editors made the case a statehood argument: the Santa Fe New Mexican found it "gratifying" that the lynching was averted and later called the case "another argument in favor of statehood for New Mexico." The Optic's "Judge Lynch" editorial said a lynching after "the recent riot at Raton" would have been taken as proof of the territory's "unfitness for self-government." Outside the territory the El Paso News, reprinted in San Antonio, said New Mexico "has set an example to the entire country," and Arizona's Copper Era called it "the first attempt in years" to lynch prisoners from a New Mexico jail.

Accounts of the shooting, all from trainmen, officers or wire writers, differ: the wire had insults and a shot through the neck, the Optic a blow by the marshal and a head wound, and the White Oaks Eagle a blow and instant death. The shooter appears as Mimms and as Minns, and the El Paso News said in October that the indicted mob leaders "pleaded guilty," while the Santa Fe New Mexican said they were "found guilty."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of dining-car porters at Raton
bases: A mob of nearly two hundred broke into the Raton jail to lynch five Black porters, who had been removed (A7, A6, A24).

A mob of some two hundred, acting to avenge the marshal's killing, broke into the jail illegally (A7, A24), but no one was killed because the sheriff had removed the prisoners (A6); it was an attempted lynching.
Independent local reports (Las Vegas Optic, Santa Fe New Mexican, White Oaks Eagle) and the wire agree that a mob forced the jail and found the prisoners gone (A7, A15, A16, A8).

accounts.label: Wire report (Raton, June 11)
accounts.gist: Three Black men insulted the marshal and one shot him through the neck from behind a saloon screen when he tried to arrest them; a mob of 200 was hunting the shooter to hang him.

accounts.label: Trainmen's account (Las Vegas Daily Optic)
accounts.gist: Drinking porters were refused craps under a saloon rule barring Black men from gambling; the marshal knocked two down and one fired through the passage door, hitting him in the head.

accounts.label: White Oaks Eagle
accounts.gist: Delayed porters were drinking when a difficulty arose and the watchman struck one; Wm Mimms then shot him in the head, killing him instantly.

accounts.label: Sheriff Littrell (to the Optic)
accounts.gist: He removed the prisoners with help from Raton citizens; the marshal's brothers wanted no violence; had the mob secured the prisoners all would have been lynched.

accounts.label: Territorial editors
accounts.gist: The prompt action of officials averted a lynching and the mob leaders were punished, showing New Mexico was law-abiding and fit for statehood.

framing.detail: Distant papers ran the Raton wire under 'Mob After a Negro', 'Mob Chasing Negro', 'Three Negroes in Danger', calling the shooting 'most cold-blooded'.
Las Vegas Daily Optic calls the porter a murderer but calls a lynching a 'disgrace' and prints the trainmen's account of the saloon's color rule.
Santa Fe New Mexican editorials praise officials for averting the lynching and use the case as 'another argument in favor of statehood'.
Optic 'Judge Lynch', Albuquerque Weekly Citizen, El Paso News (via San Antonio Light) and Copper Era praise punishment of the mob leaders.
